One Vercel service: a Fastify 5 API that also serves the compiled React SPA · PostgreSQL 16 · every box maps to a file in this repository
framework: fastify · root: . · one runtime, one origin
apps/web/src → built at deploy time, served as bytes
no message queue · no worker fleet · no Redis / cache
no object storage · no second service
no authentication at all — the deliberate current state (frame 08)
the SPA is bytes served by this same process
solid border — implemented and exercised by tests
dashed border — conditional or development-only path
red — known limitation or deployment caveat
grey — outside this codebase (browser, platform, DB)
text on an arrow — the mechanism, never an assumption
2. Fastify answers with the compiled index.html
3. the bundle loads and asks GET /api/dashboard
4. same origin, same process, same DATABASE_URL
5. TanStack Query caches it for 15s, then a poll refreshes

RelayOS is a single Node process (Fastify) that owns both the JSON API and the built single-page app, persists every entity in PostgreSQL through one async `Db` interface, and derives its delivery-governance behaviour — SLA clocks, turnover gates, acceptance ladders, ship gates — from rows in
that same database rather than from a workflow engine.
01 · Deployment — how a commit becomes a running service
Build time — never on a request
TypeScript compilation · Vite bundling · SPA embedding
dependency installation · migration SQL bundled as text
the build machine needs devDependencies; the runtime does not
ensure operator + Studio board · listen on PORT
DATABASE_URL — required; there is no SQLite fallback in production
apps/api/src/entrypoints/index.ts — the deployed entry: owns the listening socket
api/index.js → dist/entrypoints/vercel.js — a (req,res) handler retained for a
function-shaped deployment and for tests; it awaits app.ready() because listen() does
Every deployment URL on this Vercel scope answers 302 → vercel.com/login
(Deployment Protection / Vercel Authentication). Build and deploy checks pass;
runtime behaviour could not be observed from outside the account.
GitHub Actions runs in parallel, not instead

ci.yml → verify: guards · typecheck · 283 tests · PostgreSQL 16 · build · screen smoke · browser e2e · docker + single-service-build (production install and the service's own build command) + Node 24 compatibility.
nav rail · command palette · live pulse
one file per route, lazy-loaded chunks
deep links work because the API answers any browser path with index.html
const BASE = '/api' — relative, so there is no CORS and no base URL to configure
request(): JSON headers, credentials:'omit', a per-call deadline via AbortSignal
throws ApiError (status + code + envelope) or NetworkError (never reached the API)
api.* — ~60 typed methods: api.projects, api.createTask, api.clocks …
QueryClient: staleTime 15s · refetchOnWindowFocus off · retry once, never on 4xx
lib/query-state.ts → useQueryState / useMutationFailure: loading | error | empty | data
lib/live.ts → useLiveUpdates: polls GET /api/changes and invalidates stale keys
components: ApiFailure, QueryFailure, ErrorBoundary, LivePulse, TaskDrawer
Pages — what each one shows and the endpoints it calls
1 user clicks Projects → <Route path="/projects"> renders pages/Projects.tsx (lazy chunk)
3 api.projects → request('/projects') → fetch('/api/projects') — same origin, no base URL
4 Fastify route GET /api/projects → repositories/query.ts mapProject → ok(rows) → {"data":[…],"meta":…}
5 react-query caches under ['projects'], useQueryState picks the branch, the table renders
6 a create mutation invalidates ['projects'] and ['dashboard'] — the two views cannot disagree
03 · Backend — one Fastify process, four internal layers
apps/api/src · routing → business logic → data access → PostgreSQL; no service/repository ceremony that the code does not have
content-type parsers: JSON as text, '*' lenient
onRequest: stamp start time, drop empty content-type
@fastify/static — only when a dist dir exists
3 call a service or a SQL query
and rendered by the single error handler
clocks.ts — SLA timers: start, pause, resolve, sweep
db/types.ts Db { all, get, run, exec, tx }
health, live, ready, metrics, meta, users — ops surface
tasks, checklist, comments, turnover, acceptance — work
qa, releases, ship gate, acknowledgements — quality
dashboard, activity, notifications, insights — read models
changes, audit, search, suggest — history & lookup
lifecycle, comms, legal, docs, change-requests — governance
POST /api/tasks create a task (zod body, key generated)
PATCH /api/tasks/:id update, after a scope check
POST /api/tasks/:id/acceptance one step of the acceptance ladder
POST /api/clocks/sweep manual sweep (same code as cron)
POST /api/releases new release; PATCH moves its state
What is genuinely layered, and what is not
Layered: HTTP handlers (routes/index.ts) → business rules (services/, domain/) → data access (db/ + raw SQL in handlers).
Not layered: there is no ORM, no repository class per entity, and no dependency-injection container. Handlers call SQL directly for simple reads;
services own multi-step writes and invariant checks. repositories/query.ts is a mapper module (TASK_SELECT, mapProject, mapClient…), not a repository layer.
Consequence: fewer indirections to read, and SQL is visible where it runs — at the cost of some duplication in SELECT lists.
socket → Fastify router → onRequest hooks (start time, identity) → handler → validation → service/SQL → response serialisation
→ onResponse hooks (log line, RED metrics, change_log row) → socket. An error at any point unwinds to setErrorHandler,
which renders the same JSON envelope for validation failures, not-found, conflicts and unexpected 500s.
17 migrations · 81 tables · core entities drawn with real columns; every FK below exists in db/migrations/pg/*.sql
id TEXT PK · slug TEXT UNIQUE · name TEXT NOT NULL

client_id → clients(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT N:1
deal_id → deals(id) SET NULL · owner_id → users(id)
id TEXT PK · key TEXT UNIQUE (RLY-142)
project_id → projects CASCADE · board_id → boards CASCADE
column_id → columns · parent_id → tasks (self) · assignee_id → users
id TEXT PK · project_id → projects(id) CASCADE N:1
id TEXT PK · project_id → projects CASCADE N:1
release_id TEXT — deliberately no FK (reports outlive releases)
id TEXT PK · task_id → tasks CASCADE
UNIQUE (task_id, step) — one row per rung per task
id TEXT PK · project_id → projects CASCADE
id TEXT PK · project_id → projects CASCADE
position INT — ordering only, not a foreign key
id TEXT PK · email TEXT UNIQUE · full_name
every created_by / actor_id column points here
id TEXT PK · client_id → clients RESTRICT N:1
id TEXT PK · key TEXT UNIQUE (inbound, triage, tech_consult…)
id TEXT PK · client_id → clients CASCADE N:1
id TEXT PK · key TEXT UNIQUE · name
id TEXT PK · gate_id → turnover_gates CASCADE N:1
CHECK (task_id IS NOT NULL OR project_phase_id IS NOT NULL)
clocks: id PK · key UNIQUE · scope · anchor_event
entity_type + entity_id — polymorphic, NO foreign key
audit_log: id BIGINT identity · actor_id · action
change_log: id BIGINT identity · method · path · created_at
both append-only; neither has a foreign key (survives deletes)
Notation and the rest of the schema

FK → table(column) with its ON DELETE rule · UNIQUE constraints shown where they carry business meaning · polymorphic references (sla_timers.entity_id, qa_reports.release_id) are stated as such because no foreign key enforces them.

The remaining tables — board columns, labels, task_comments, checklist items, handoffs, time_entries, teams, comm_* , legal_* , lifecycle_* , insight_dismissals, rate_limit_counters — follow the same shape and are enumerated in the traceability file.
05 · Request lifecycle — two end-to-end sequences, with the file at every step
read path: GET /api/projects · write path: POST /api/tasks
HTTP/1.1 200 · content-type: application/json · cache-control: no-store (vercel.json header rule for /api/*)
onResponse hook appends one change_log row, so other tabs refresh.
400 bad_request — zod issues, or title shorter than 4 characters
400 — board has no column with that key · 404 — board not found
409 — key collision (UNIQUE) · 500 — anything uncaught, rendered as the same envelope
06 · Delivery workflow — what the code enforces, not what a brochure claims
Sales pipeline — 12 stages seeded into pipeline_stages (db/scaffolding.ts)
A deal holds stage_id (FK, NOT NULL) and moves by PATCH /api/deals/:id. The stage list is data; no server-side guard restricts which stage follows which.
Client lifecycle — 18 stages with guarded transitions (services/lifecycle.ts)
anything absent from the table is refused · unmet prerequisites block the move
lifecycle_evidence rows are required before a guarded stage advances
one acceptance_records row per task per step · UNIQUE (task_id, step)
a step cannot be skipped: the service checks the ladder index before writing
each step stores actor_id, evidence text and decided_at
8 machine rules: has_description · has_assignee · estimate_set · review_approved
gates are rows (turnover_gates.scope = task | phase | project)
checks are rows (turnover_checks.status = pending | pass | fail | waived)
a task's turnover_state: draft → in_review → passed | failed | waived
planning → in_qa → demo_ready → demo_done → approved → shipped | rolled_back
evaluateShipGate() refuses to ship while a required check is open
markShipped() writes shipped_at and the ship_acknowledgements rows
a policy (sla_clocks) names the anchor event, target, warn and stretch hours
starting work creates an sla_timers row: due_at, warn_at, outcome='running'
sweepTimers() marks overdue timers 'missed' · pause/resume/resolve are endpoints
What the UI shows versus what the server enforces
Enforced: lifecycle transitions, acceptance ladder, turnover checks, ship gate,
SLA outcomes, unique keys, foreign keys, CHECK constraints.
Display only: pipeline ordering, colours, progress bars, KPI tiles.
Where the workflow state actually lives
Everything is a row: a transition is an UPDATE, and history is the audit trail.
07 · Background jobs — three triggers, one sweep, no queue
GET, bearer token compared with timingSafeEqual
503 if CRON_SECRET is unset — it is never silently disabled
not started by the serverless handler
so a daily cron is not the only chance
SELECT timers WHERE outcome='running' AND due_at <= now
idempotent: only already-due running rows move
failure: the cron endpoint reports the error; the inline sweep swallows it so a
user request is never failed by bookkeeping — the cron remains the alerter
Other time-shaped work, and what does not exist
change_log: one row per successful write, appended by an onResponse hook (not a job)
legal: renewal_notice_days stored, no reminder sender exists
comms: follow-ups are rows with due dates; nothing dispatches them
There is no queue, no worker, no scheduler table and no retry queue. A job that must be durable would have to be built, not configured.

The only time-based invariant the product needs is "a clock that passed its due date is marked missed". It is one UPDATE, so it runs wherever the process happens to be awake — cron, interval, or a request — rather than requiring a worker tier.
08 · Security — the exact current implementation, including what is missing
auth/ · lib/rate-limit.ts · app.ts hooks · db constraints · vercel.json headers
rate limits: 1200/min global · 30/min auth · 240/min write (per IP)
body limit 2 MB · JSON parsed as text then validated
every query parameterised; the dialect layer rewrites ? → $n
FOREIGN KEY / CHECK / UNIQUE constraints carry the invariants
cron secret compared with timingSafeEqual · no-store on /api/*
no authentication: no sign-in, no password, no session, no cookie
no CSRF token (nothing to protect: credentials are omitted)
no RBAC in force — the operator resolves as role 'admin'
no per-user quota: limits are per IP, and trust proxy is on
no encryption at rest in the app; that is the database's job
no signed URLs: there is no object storage in this system
Anyone who can reach the URL can read and write every record.
The only gate is Vercel Deployment Protection in front of the
deployment — a platform setting, not application code.
Every mutation is attributable to one operator row (usr_owner),
so the audit trail answers 'what changed', not 'who changed it'.
This is a stated product decision, not an oversight: /api/auth/login
a fixed-window limiter over an in-process Map
three budgets: global / auth / write, keyed by IP
when the database is shared the counter store can be
429 with retry-after; the frontend renders it as an ApiError
every statement is parameterised — no string interpolation of input
the portability guard checks statements on both engines in CI
identifiers are never taken from a request
ORDER BY / LIMIT fragments come from allow-lists in the handlers
read from process.env at access time (config is a Proxy)
no secret is logged: the access log records route, status, ms, actor
no secret is committed; .env files are gitignored and CI secret-scans
Audit trail — two files, two purposes
audit_log (0003_intel.sql): entity_type, entity_id, action, before_json, after_json, actor_id, request_id — rich history, written by the handlers that need it.
change_log (0017_change_log.sql): method, path, entity_type, entity_id — one row for every successful mutation, appended by an onResponse hook, so the live-update feed cannot go blind.
Both are append-only and have no foreign keys, so a deleted entity keeps its history. Neither stores request bodies or credentials.
09 · Failure — what actually happens at each break point
lib/misconfigured.ts · app.ts setErrorHandler / setNotFoundHandler · db/index.ts · entrypoints/vercel.ts
no DATABASE_URL → getDb() throws instead of creating a file in /tmp
recordBootFailure(stage, err) stores the reason on the instance
every response is 503: JSON for /api/*, a setup page for a browser
the page names the missing variable and the remedy — nothing else
zod safeParse → 400 bad_request with the issue list
a constraint violation maps to 409 conflict
unknown route: 404 not_found for /api/*, index.html otherwise
the pool rejects; the request fails at the query
setErrorHandler renders 500 with the same envelope
the detail is hidden unless INTERNAL_ERROR_DETAIL=1
with a shared store the limiter survives; membership is not cached
the July outage: @fastify/static imported at module scope pulled
an ESM-only transitive into a CommonJS require → ERR_REQUIRE_ESM
while the module was loading, before any route existed
now: the import is inside the branch that needs it, and a failure
is thrown with the directory named · node:sqlite likewise lazy
cron: the error surfaces as a 5xx from the endpoint, with a log line
inline sweep: swallowed on purpose — a user request must not fail
idempotent by construction: only running, already-due rows move
no retry queue exists, so the next trigger is the retry
ApiError: the API answered with a code and a message
NetworkError: the request never completed (offline, blocked, CORS)
a deadline aborts slow calls via AbortSignal
ApiFailure / QueryFailure render the reason and a retry
ErrorBoundary catches a render crash; the retry is per-route
process is up, uptime in seconds
pool: pg.Pool max 10, idleTimeout 30s, connectionTimeout — sized for many
tx(fn): one client held for the duration, rolled back on throw
migrations: schema_migrations ledger with a checksum per file, applied on
boot unless SKIP_MIGRATE=1 · 17 files, bundled as text at build time
npm run backup:verify: a restore drill comparing 81 tables and every row
CI runs the drill on each push; the last run compared 2330 rows
no point-in-time recovery is configured inside the app — that is the
The server retries nothing. The client retries once, and only for 5xx or transport failures (a 4xx is a bug, and retrying it hides the bug). There is no circuit breaker and no bulkhead.
npm run verify · apps/api/test (24 files) · scripts/ · .github/workflows/ci.yml
npm run verify — the local gate, in order
crud · editing · http · domain — behaviour through the API
clock-scope · clocks-pause · shipgate · lifecycle — the rules
resilience — pool exhaustion, failing statements, timeouts
auth — identity resolution and the retired endpoints
vercel · platform-launcher · service-entry — the deployment shapes
module-format — a dependency cannot break module loading
deployment-layout — dist-only boot, SPA served, deep links
applies all 17 migrations to an empty cluster
seeds, then drives governance / auth / resilience / HTTP
19 tests in the current run · 2 skipped in SQLite mode by design
the same suite proves the SQL portability guard is not theoretical
scripts/smoke-web.mjs — server-renders every screen against real data,
and asserts every failure state names the real cause
scripts/verify-web-routing.mjs — deep links, assets, JSON 404 for /api
scripts/production-boot.mjs — boots dist with no auth env at all
CI only: headless Chromium e2e, Docker build, Docker + PostgreSQL start
GitHub Actions — three workflows worth knowing
ci.yml · verify — lockfile integrity (root and web), dependency audit,
secret scan, architecture guards, strict typecheck, SQLite migrations from
empty, 283 tests, PostgreSQL 16 conformance, backup drill, edge-case registry,
web build, screen smoke, Chromium e2e, production boot, Docker build and run
ci.yml · single-service-build — production-mode install, then the service's own
build command, asserting the entrypoints and SPA artefacts exist
ci.yml · node-24 compatibility · traceability · backup.yml (scheduled drill)
A green build is not a deployment
CI proves the code compiles, migrates, serves and persists.
It does not prove the platform can start the process, that the platform's
node runtime matches the one under test, or that environment variables exist.
The deployment-specific checks are: single-service-build (install + build
exactly as the platform does it) and service-entry / platform-launcher tests
(spawn the built entry and drive it over a socket).
What remains unproven is the platform itself — see frame 13.
The regression that motivated half of this file

The Vercel outage was invisible locally: this workstation's Node can require() an ES module, the platform's could not. Every module-format assertion therefore runs a child process with --no-experimental-require-module, against the real installed packages — a guard shaped exactly like the failure.
11 · Technology — what is used, where, and what removing it would cost
declared dependencies only; nothing below is aspirational
React 19 — the view layer; every screen is a component tree
Vite 7 — bundler and dev server; produces apps/web/dist
react-router 7 — client routing; deep links rely on the API's fallback
TanStack Query 5 — server-state cache, retries, invalidation
recharts — charts on the dashboard and intelligence screens
lucide-react — icon set (a closed union, so icons cannot be strings)
Remove Query and every screen hand-rolls loading, cache and retry.
Node 22.18+ / 24 — runtime; the entry is TypeScript with .ts specifiers
TypeScript 5 — types only; tsc emits dist, no bundler in the API
Fastify 5 — HTTP server, hooks, schema-free routing, per-route handlers
zod 4 — request body validation in routes
pg 8 — the PostgreSQL driver and pool
Remove Fastify and every hook, error shape and lifecycle is rebuilt.
PostgreSQL 16 — the only store in a deployment
SQL migrations — 17 ordered files, checksummed ledger
node:sqlite — development and unit tests only, loaded lazily
node:test — the test runner; no Jest, no Vitest
embedded-postgres — a real PG 16 binary for tests and CI
Remove PostgreSQL and the product loses concurrent writes,
transactions, constraints and every governance query at once.
Vercel — hosts the single service; services mode + cron
GitHub Actions — the gate: tests, PostgreSQL, docker, e2e
Docker / Compose — the alternative container path, built on CI
Prometheus text exposition — /api/metrics, no agent shipped
Remove Vercel and the app still runs as a container or with
npm start: entrypoints/index.ts owns a socket in both cases.
No ORM: SQL is written and read directly, so the queries are reviewable and the
migration files are the schema. Cost: SELECT lists repeat.
No Redis: rate-limit counters live in a Map, or in a table when instances share a database.
No message broker: the only asynchronous work is a sweep that can run anywhere.
No API gateway, no service mesh, no second deployable.
Declared but unused — say it before it is found
argon2 is still in apps/api/package.json. Authentication was removed, and nothing
imports it: grep for 'argon2' in apps/api/src returns nothing.
It is a leftover of the password-login era (migration 0014, local_credentials).
Removing it is a one-line change with a lockfile update; it is left in place here
so the dependency change is not mixed into an architecture commit.
Node engines: >=22.18.0 <25 — the floor is default type stripping (.ts entrypoints), the ceiling keeps CI and local development on the same line.
Fastify 5 · pg 8 · zod 4 · React 19 · react-router 7 · TanStack Query 5 · Vite 7 · TypeScript 5 · PostgreSQL 16.
The one pinned exactly is @fastify/static 10.1.3, because 10.1.4 pulls an ESM-only transitive into a CommonJS graph (frame 09).

Tests, in the order they matter

package.json → vercel.json → apps/api/src/app.ts → apps/api/src/routes/index.ts (skim by group) → services/tasks.ts → db/migrate.ts + one migration → apps/web/src/main.tsx + App.tsx → lib/api.ts → one page.
13 · Known gaps — stated plainly, with the evidence for each
every line below was read out of the repository at the inspected commit
No authentication. Anyone who can reach the URL can read and write.
One identity for every write: usr_owner, role 'admin'.
no sign-in path is mounted, so none of it is in force.
Per-user attribution is therefore impossible today.
The audit trail answers what changed, not who changed it.
Implemented as data, not as an integration
Comms: /api/comms/providers reports whether SMTP or WhatsApp is
configured; threads, messages and follow-ups are stored; nothing sends.
E-signature: esignStatus() reports DocuSign / Dropbox Sign config;
decisions and manual uploads are recorded, no API call is made.
Legal renewals: renewal_notice_days is stored; no reminder job exists.
Partner console: devices, entitlements and usage are tracked as rows;
nothing provisions or revokes at a provider.
Technical debt a reviewer will find
argon2 is declared in apps/api/package.json and imported nowhere.
routes/index.ts is 3,370 lines: ~100 handlers in one module.
Rate limiting is per IP and in memory unless the shared
Migrations run on boot; a failing migration blocks cold start
The web app has no unit tests: rendering is covered by the
server-render smoke suite and the Chromium e2e run.
Docker is built and started on CI, not deployed anywhere.
Needs verification — do not claim it
1. The Node version the Vercel function actually runs. The failing runtime
demonstrably lacked require(esm); the fix no longer depends on it either way.
2. Whether the production environment sets DATABASE_URL and CRON_SECRET.
3. Whether the post-fix deployment boots and serves /api/live. Every URL on
this scope is behind Vercel Deployment Protection, so it could not be
Things that look like debt and are not
sessions_new / sla_timers_new in migrations 0010 and 0014 are temporary rebuild
tables: SQLite cannot alter a CHECK in place, so the table is recreated and
renamed. The final schema has no *_new table.
apps/api/src/auth/*.ts is not dead code: the operator middleware, scope
resolution and requireProjectAccess are all on the request path.
SQLite is not a fallback in production: a serving runtime with no DATABASE_URL
throws rather than creating a file (test: 'a serving runtime without
DATABASE_URL throws instead of creating a file').

RelayOS is a working, well-tested single-service application with a real relational schema and real governance rules. Its weak points are the ones the product deliberately chose: no authentication, no external integrations behind the modelled workflows, and no queue. Its engineering strength is that the failure modes are written down
and tested — module loading, boot failure, unknown routes, dead databases, stale screens — rather than discovered in production.

Source of truth: the commit recorded in docs/architecture/RELAYOS_ARCHITECTURE_TRACEABILITY.md. Every path, symbol, route, table and script named on this board was read from the repository at that commit; nothing here comes from a README, an earlier conversation, or an assumption about how a system like this usually looks.
